Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Stuffing the paper into the cup
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is the source paper visibly stuffed inside the source cup in the edited image?
node.criteria: Pass if the edited image shows the paper from the source image placed inside the cup from the source image, with visible evidence it has been stuffed into it. Fail if the matched paper and cup are assessable and the paper is visibly outside the cup or only resting nearby or on its rim. Unknown if the source objects cannot be reliably matched in the edited image, or their relationship cannot be assessed.
node.binding: Identify the requested paper and cup by their visual and contextual roles in the source image, allowing their appearance to change in the edited image. Judge whether that paper is stuffed inside that cup; do not require exact color or shape matches.

node_traces.evidence: The source paper and cup are visible, but the edited image does not reliably show the same cup or paper: it shows a hand holding a blue printed item near a round object. Their relationship cannot be assessed as the requested paper being stuffed into the source cup.

s2: The node’s conservative identity gate is appropriate: the edited frame shows a hand-held blue printed item and a reddish round object, not clearly the source paper and blue cup, so the trace’s unknown is supported by the images. Do not force `no` from the aggregate reference label; it is not atomic ground truth, and the rubric explicitly keeps insufficient evidence unresolved. The metric failure is unresolved coverage, not a transport or schema failure (the node executed validly, was queried, and returned valid uncertainty). For typed edits, investigate whether the binding/criteria can use stronger contextual and relational cues to distinguish identity from superficial color or shape, while retaining the requirement that both source objects be reliably matched before judging progress. Clarify how to assess visible partial progress when identity is supported despite appearance changes, and keep unknown when identity or placement genuinely cannot be established. The high-confidence unknown is not itself evidence of a bad decision; avoid lowering confidence or relaxing the evidence threshold merely to match this one reference.
